body:
Hey @luxlogica!

I'm just walking through my thought process explaining why our installation process looks like it does today. That said, I'm absolutely open to rethinking how it works. 😄 

> Installation via manually downloading a binary and then manually editing the shell's config is very user-unfriendly.

The binaries are provided as a final resort. We are working to increase the [number of registries](https://repology.org/project/starship/versions) that starship is available on, but we are available on Homebrew for macOS, Linuxbrew or Linux, and have plans to add Starship to Scoop and Chocolatey for Windows.

> On top of that, no mechanism exists for quick auto-update - which is important when dealing with a fast-moving and rapidly advancing project like Starship. Right now, the user is expected to observe the repository, and manually download + re-install the binary whenever there is a new release.

All of these registries have their own updating solutions, and often disallow binaries that self-update because they clash with the update mechanism provided by the registry.

> All other prompt themes - including Spaceship, which Starship is based off - are installable this way, and right now the Starship installation process stands out as unusually cumbersome (and is possibly slowing adoption).

The trouble with comparing Starship's installation process with Spaceship ZSH is that we are distributing binaries for use on various architectures and operating systems. There's no one-size-fits-all installation like there are for other prompts.

All of that said, I absolutely agree that there is more friction in the installation process than there should be, and I would be open to rethinking installation.

These are the steps I think would be necessary when installing via prompt package managers:
- The user installs a starship package for their prompt (`starship/zsh` for the oh-my-zsh package for instance)
	```
	antigen theme starship/zsh 
	```
- Identify the OS and architecture of the system
- If not already downloaded, download the starship binary matching the system and version of the prompt package
	- In order to allow the prompt to be versioned by the prompt package manager, the prompt distribution would need to be versioned in parallel with starship binary versions to allow for the user to install past versions of the binary + prompt combination
	- We could possibly include the release binaries in the prompt package. It would make the download long, but that might be an easy way to avoid having to add download logic to the prompt.

> Own Script-Based Installation: having scripts - for each shell - that the user can download and run, with functions that will automatically download and install (and maybe update) Starship.

I'd absolutely be interested in creating a one-liner installation script! Most registries don't allow self-updating binaries, so it would either have to be updated by a separate "starship version manager" binary, or be built into starship, but be optionally included at build-time. I think this is a valuable option to provide but does bring about its own complexities:
- Managing `$PATH`
- Correct binary selection (OS + architecture combination)
- Installing the prompt on the correct shell
- Uninstallation
- "Auto-update"
	Since starship runs as a prompt and doesn't include any sort of daemon, we can't perform operations in the background (unless we use jobs..? 🤔). Oh-my-zsh freezes the prompt on startup to check for updates, and I personally find that to be annoying. I'd like to avoid doing that if possible.

@matchai The prospect of having Starship installable by the shell plugin managers is really exciting - and judging by your outlined steps, very doable. The only 'tricky' or troublesome step seems to be  identifying the environment (OS, shell, etc.).

I remember a while ago installing a theme that ran a 'configuration wizard' on its first run. We could have a similar approach: have a 'wizard' that downloads the appropriate binary and add the necessary configurations on the first run.

I and I'm sure others would really appreciate it if you could make add the starship to ubuntu repos, fumbling around with binaries is inelegant.

While there is more friction than other prompts I don't think It is too annoying for people. I don't personalty like installation scripts very much. I think they tend to be brittle, and sometimes do something the final user did not want to do.
